senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: sin which is committed as the result of ignorance
glosses: to sin without knowing that one has sinned

senses.def: to refuse to recognize the validity of something
the process of causing something not to continue
to rise up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands
senses.comment: It is possible that ἀκαταστασία in Luke 21:9 denotes merely unsettled conditions, but it is far more likely to carry the meaning of ‘insurrections’ and ‘revolts.’

senses.def: violent opposition to someone or something, involving mob action
pertaining to that which is different in kind or class from all other entities
to adjourn a court proceeding until a later time
glosses: to stop a hearing and put it off until later

senses.def: pertaining to not corresponding to a comparable merit or worth

annual plant that can reach 50 cm in height; has fine leaves; yellow flowers form a shape like a covered cup; leaves and seeds have a pleasant, spicy smell; Anethum graveolens; garden herb, used in cooking
senses.comment: In designating ‘dill’ as well as ἡδύοσμον ‘mint,’ πήγανον ‘rue,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called dill.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which corresponds in form and structure to something else, either as an anticipation of a later reality or as a fulfillment of a prior type
motion away from a reference point with emphasis upon the departure, but without implications as to any resulting state of separation or rupture
to go out of existence
(an idiom, literally: to go back to what lies behind) to cease being a follower or disciple of
glosses: to no longer be a disciple

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to go after strange flesh) to engage in unnatural sexual intercourse
senses.comment: Though in some societies homosexuality is extremely rare, there are always ways of talking about it, though frequently the expressions may seem to be quite vulgar.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to return to oneself) to go back to one’s place or abode
glosses: to go back to one’s place

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with the implication of something deserved

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an extremely short unit of time
pertaining to what has not been made by someone
to cause something to be known as certain
glosses: to prove to be true and certain
senses.comment: Philippians 1:7 βεβαίωσις may denote either the process of making known something in such a way as to confirm its truth or the process of causing people to think about something and to accept it as trustworthy, in which case βεβαίωσις might also be classified in Domain 31 Hold a View, Believe, Trust, Subdomain G Accept as True.

senses.def: watery mud, with an additional feature of filth and uncleanness
(derivative of γραῦς ‘old woman,’ not occurring in the NT) characteristic of old women
pertaining to being to the right of some point of reference
senses.comment: For another interpretation of δεξιός as part of an idiom in Mark 10:37, see 87.34.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: an abbreviated reference to a person’s right hand, which is generally the dominant hand; positive associations as opposed to the left
senses.comment: The expression in Matthew 6:3 is idiomatic and means not letting others know about the good which one does (see 28.74). The right hand is often spoken of idiomatically as ‘the good hand’ or ‘the strong hand.’ Sometimes it is called ‘the mouth hand,’ that is to say, the hand which one uses in eating.|For δεξιά in the idiom δεξιὰς δίδωμι ‘to give the right hand’ (Galatians 2:9), see 34.42.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of δεξιός[b] ‘right hand,’ 8.32) power, with the added implication of authority
(an idiom, literally: to give right hands) to acknowledge an agreement establishing some relation, normally involving the actual practice of shaking hands

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to make a judgment on the basis of careful and detailed information

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to judge something to be better than something else, and hence, to prefer
senses.comment: Superiority is often expressed in terms of ‘being better,’ but in some languages it is designated by means of a phrase meaning ‘to surpass,’ so that the question in 1 Corinthians 4:7 may be rendered as ‘who judges that you surpass others?’

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to judge that there is a difference or distinction
glosses: to judge that there is a difference
senses.comment: In some languages it may be best to render this statement in Acts 15:9 as ‘he did not think that we and they are different.’

senses.def: to think that something may not be true or certain
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘doubt’ is expressed by means of idioms, for example, ‘to have two thoughts’ or ‘to think only perhaps’ or ‘to believe only a little’ or ‘to question one’s heart about.’

senses.def: to dispute with someone on the basis of different judgments
to express disapproval of what someone has done
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret the meaning of διακρίνομαι in Acts 11:2 as being merely adverse judgment, but since this judgment was clearly voiced, διακρίνομαι implies more than mere judgment. The direct expression of an adverse judgment may be best rendered in English as ‘to criticize.’

senses.def: to move away from, with the possible implication of definitiveness of separation (particularly in contexts relating to persons)
to follow with haste, and presumably with intensity of effort, in order to catch up with, for friendly or hostile purpose
to move quickly and energetically toward some objective
senses.comment: In Philippians 3:14 διώκω is to be understood in a literal sense, though the entire context is figurative. For interpreting the expression κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω as an idiom, see 89.56.

senses.def: to systematically organize a program to oppress and harass people
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to persecute’ is simply ‘to cause to suffer,’ but persecution is also expressed in terms of ‘to be mean to’ or ‘to threaten’ or ‘to chase from place to place.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of διώκω[a] ‘to pursue,’ 15.158) to do something with intense effort and with definite purpose or goal
(an idiom, literally: to pursue to a goal, to press toward a goal) to strive energetically for some purpose
glosses: to press on with the purpose of

senses.def: a marker of condition, with the implication of reduced probability

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is somewhat conditional and simultaneous with another point of time
a marker of the possibility of any number of occurrences of some event

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of sincerity as an expression of pure or unadulterated motives
to break off a part
(derivative of ἐλαία[a] ‘olive tree,’ 3.9) a number of olive trees planted in a garden or grove
senses.comment: In Acts 1:12, it may be well to employ the more common designation for ‘the hill called The Olive Grove,’ namely, ‘Hill of Olives’ or ‘Mount of Olives’ (see 3.9).

senses.def: to make fun of someone by pretending that he is not what he is or by imitating him in a distorted manner

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to trick someone into thinking or doing something and thus to make a fool of such a person
senses.comment: In Matthew 2:16 ἐμπαίζω would seem to carry two closely related meanings, namely ‘to deceive’ and also ‘to make a fool of,’ and therefore it may be quite appropriate to translate this portion of Matthew 2:16 as ‘when Herod realized that the wise men had deceived him and made a fool of him.’

senses.def: to exist, with respect to particular circumstances

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the contents of the stomach ejected through the mouth
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘vomit’ is a descriptive phrase based upon a verb describing the process of vomiting, for example, ‘that which is vomited’ or ‘food that flows out of the mouth from the stomach.’

senses.def: a messenger sent to Paul from the Philippian church
not recalling information concerning some particular matter
pertaining to being glorious or wonderful, in view of being conspicuous and self-evident

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: extension of time up to and beyond an expected point
the state of something being in addition to what already exists
senses.comment: The sequence ἔτι τε καί in Luke 14:26 is clearly emphatic, so that one might well render the expression ἔτι τε καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἑαυτοῦ as ‘and he himself as well.’

senses.def: a marker of contrast, involving something contrary to expectation
appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

senses.def: behavior reflecting correct religious beliefs and attitudes
senses.comment: In a number of languages εὐσέβεια in 1 Timothy 2:2 may be appropriately translated as ‘to live as God would have us live’ or ‘to live as God has told us we should live.’

senses.def: attempting to learn something by careful investigation or searching
senses.comment: The clause ‘about how I could get information on these matters’ (Acts 25:20) may also be rendered as ‘about how I should try to find out about these matters’ or ‘about how I could learn about these matters.’

senses.def: expressing of forceful differences of opinion without necessarily having a presumed goal of seeking a solution
a state of astonishment due to both the suddenness and the unusualness of the phenomenon and with either a positive or a negative reaction
to be emotionally upset by a concern or anxiety
senses.comment: In Luke 10:41 the meanings of μεριμνάω (25.225) and θορυβάζομαι reinforce each other.

senses.def: (derivative of Ιεροσόλυμα ‘Jerusalem,’ 93.480) an inhabitant of Jerusalem
(derivative of Ἰταλία ‘Italy,’ 93.489) pertaining to Italy
the Greek transcription for a Latin word used as a name and title for a Roman emperor
a title for the Roman Emperor
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not easy to distinguish between terms for rulers such as ‘governor,’ ‘king,’ and ‘emperor.’ Sometimes one can only attempt a measure of distinction by indicating relative power or dominion. For example, ‘emperor’ may be rendered as ‘the great ruler’ or ‘the most important chief of all.’

senses.def: (derivative of καταγγέλλω ‘to proclaim,’ 33.204) one who proclaims

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.def: to cause something to pass through the mouth and into the stomach
senses.comment: The saying about ‘straining out a fly and swallowing a camel’ refers to gross unawareness of inconsistencies in one’s behavior, but in translating it is far better to preserve the intentional hyperbole, since it is one which can be readily grasped. As an aid to the reader, one can refer to the fact that in the list of unclean animals in, the fly or gnat is the smallest and the camel is the largest.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of καταπίνω[a] ‘to swallow,’ 23.45) to cause the complete and sudden destruction of someone or something
(a figurative extension of meaning of καταπίνω[a] ‘to swallow,’ 23.45) to cause the complete cessation of a state
(an idiom, literally: to be swallowed up by grief) to be so overcome with grief as to despair
glosses: to grieve to the point of giving up

senses.def: to live or dwell in a place in an established or settled manner
senses.comment: The quotation from in Acts 1:20 normally requires a literal rendering, but the entire passage is figurative.

senses.def: (derivative of κιθαρίζω ‘to play a lyre,’ 6.84) one who plays the lyre, a small stringed harp-like instrument held in the hands and plucked
to strike or beat with the fist, either once or repeatedly
(a figurative extension of meaning of κολαφίζω[a] ‘to beat with the fist,’ 19.7) to cause injury or weakness or possibly a circumstantial difficulty
senses.comment: Though differences of interpretation exist concerning the meaning of ‘a thorn in my flesh’ (2 Corinthians 12:7), especially since some scholars have felt that this must refer to some kind of physical disability, it seems more likely to assume that it refers to some special personal circumstance such as the opposition Paul encountered in preaching the gospel, a reference suggested by 2 Corinthians 12:10 (see also 22.20).|Without some clear understanding of the reference of ‘a thorn in my flesh,’ it is difficult to determine precisely how κολαφίζω is to be interpreted in 2 Corinthians 12:7.

senses.def: (derivative of κριθή ‘barley,’ 3.44) pertaining to being made or consisting of barley, a grain somewhat similar to wheat, but regarded as less desirable for food
sudden and violent gusts of winds, often from varied directions
senses.comment: In a number of languages a strong wind which causes the waves or a storm on water must be referred to by a special term. Compare, for example, the English term squall; this would mean a wind of relatively short duration but sufficiently intense so as to create relatively high waves.

senses.def: to crush by a destructive amount of vertical pressure
to be a follower or a disciple of someone, in the sense of adhering to the teachings or instructions of a leader and in promoting the cause of such a leader
senses.comment: Though many translators have attempted to employ the metaphorical significance of ‘to follow’ in the sense of ‘to be a disciple of,’ there are certain dangers in a number of languages. For example, ‘to follow’ may often have the connotation of ‘to pursue after with evil intent.’ In many languages the appropriate equivalent of ‘to follow’ (in the sense of ‘to be a disciple’) is literally ‘to accompany’ or ‘to go along with’ or ‘to be in the group of.’

senses.def: to cause someone to become a disciple or follower of
glosses: to cause people to become followers
senses.comment: In rendering μαθητεύω in Matthew 28:19 and similar contexts, it is important to avoid the implication of duress or force, that is to say, one should not translate ‘force them to be my disciples’ or ‘compel them to be my disciples.’ This might very well be implied in a literal translation of a causative such as ‘to make.’ In order to avoid a wrong implication of a causative, it may be important to use some such expression as ‘convince them to become my disciples’ or ‘urge them to be my disciples.’

senses.def: a deed of importance and power
senses.comment: In some contexts it is not possible to distinguish readily between τέρας[b] (76.7), δύναμις[c] (76.7), and μεγαλεῖον, for all may refer to miraculous events, and in a number of instances these terms are used in pairs, primarily to emphasize rather than to distinguish different kinds of miraculous events. All of these expressions may indicate a supernatural component with important religious implications, especially since the performance of such miracles implies divine power.

senses.def: to receive as one’s share in or as one’s part of
to experience some event or state, often with the implication of something negatively valued
(derivative of μισθόομαι ‘to hire,’ 57.172) the amount offered for services or paid for work done
a recompense based upon what a person has earned and thus deserves, the nature of the recompense being either positive or negative
senses.comment: In the context of Revelation 22:12, μισθός may be understood as either a positive or negative reward.

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
senses.comment: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

senses.def: the content of thinking and reasoning
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in Luke 11:17 one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’|It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking every thought captive’ (2 Corinthians 10:5), but one can often say ‘to control every thought’ or ‘to make oneself think as one should.’

senses.def: to cause a foul-smelling odor
pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect
a fast movement from one place to another
a strong military fortification
senses.comment: The term ὀχύρωμα occurs in the NT only in 2 Corinthians 10:4, where it is used figuratively of the strength of false arguments. In a number of languages it may be more satisfactory to render ὀχύρωμα as a kind of simile so as to mark this figurative usage, for example, ‘powerful weapons with which to destroy false arguments in the same way that people would destroy fortresses.’ In some languages a ‘fortress’ may be described in terms of its function, for example, ‘a place for protection’ or ‘a place to defend oneself.’ Often, however, a fortress is described in terms of its construction, for example, ‘a strong-walled place.’

senses.def: (derivative of παραδίδωμι[c] ‘to instruct,’ 33.237) the content of traditional instruction
a temporary population center consisting of an encampment
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘camp’ in the context of Hebrews 13:11 is often ‘a city of tents’ or ‘where people lived only for a short time.’

senses.def: a camp or barracks for soldiers
senses.comment: In the NT παρεμβολή[b] is used to refer to the place where Roman troops were housed in Jerusalem and to the place in Rome where soldiers who accompanied Paul were quartered. Though many languages have a set phrase or technical expression for soldiers barracks, it may be necessary in some cases to use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘where soldiers lived or where soldiers lived together.’

senses.def: (derivative of πείθω[a] ‘to persuade,’ 33.301) the means by which someone is caused to believe
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret πεισμονή in Galatians 5:8 as the actual process of persuasion, in which case πεισμονή would be classified as a nominal form corresponding to πείθω[a] (33.301). Such an interpretation would require one to render Galatians 5:8 as he who called you was not the one who persuaded you.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of περισπάομαι ‘to be drawn off from around,’ not occurring in the NT) to be so overburdened by various distractions as to be worried and anxious
(derivative of πλάσσω[a] ‘to form, to make,’ 42.31) pertaining to being false in view of being made-up or fabricated
to speak for a long time or much
an adult male advanced in years
to send someone on in the direction in which he has already been moving, with the probable implication of providing help
to accompany a person for a short distance at the beginning of a journey
to run into the presence of someone
glosses: to run into the presence of

senses.def: a supernatural power of divination known as ‘Python’
senses.comment: For πύθων as part of an idiom, see 33.285.|In most languages there seems to be no reason to borrow the term ‘Python,’ since it may be readily misunderstood. It is both more meaningful and to some extent more accurate to translate ‘a spirit of divination’ or ‘the spirit which caused her to foretell the future’ or ‘… to tell what was going to happen.’

senses.def: a large, broad sword used for both cutting and piercing
senses.comment: In a number of languages the term for ‘sword’ is simply ‘a large knife,’ but in some regions it may be called ‘a machete for killing.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of ῥομφαία[a] ‘broad sword,’ 6.32)
senses.comment: It is possible that ῥομφαία in Revelation 6:8 should be understood in its literal meaning of ‘broad sword’ (see 6.32).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: a sword goes through one’s soul) to feel the intense pain of sorrow
(a borrowing from Hebrew and Aramaic: a title for the Devil, literally: adversary) the principal supernatural evil being
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a well known proper name for the Devil as the chief of all demons. In other instances, however, he is given a descriptive name, for example, ‘the ruler of the evil spirits,’ ‘the chief of the demons,’ ‘the truly bad one,’ ‘the left-handed one’ (as the one who is opposed to all which is right or correct), ‘the no-good one,’ ‘the avaricious one.’ In some instances a term for the Devil may be highly idiomatic as, for example, ‘the barking one,’ a reference to the Devil’s presumed activity in animal guise.|Some translators have employed for ‘Devil’ the proper name Satan, but this is often not a satisfactory solution. In one language in West Africa, for example, the term Satan had already been borrowed but was understood in the sense of the culture hero of the people and not as a designation for the chief of demons.|See also Revelation 20:2.

senses.def: (a borrowing from Hebrew and Aramaic meaning literally: adversary) the usual proper name of the Devil; see also 12.34
a small boat which was normally kept aboard a larger ship and used by sailors in placing anchors, repairing the ship, or saving lives in the case of storms
senses.comment: In some languages σκάφη is equivalent to ‘rowboat’ or ‘lifeboat.’

senses.def: a cave or den generally large enough for at least temporary occupation by persons (since such places were often used for habitation or refuge by those who were refugees or thieves, σπήλαιον has in certain contexts the connotation of a ‘hideout’)
senses.comment: In Revelation 6:15 the reference of σπήλαιον is literal, since people actually hid themselves in such caves. In Matthew 21:13, however, the reference is to the Temple, which has been made a kind of ‘cave’ or ‘den,’ and since the connotation of the term suggests a ‘hideout,’ this is obviously a reflection upon the activities and motivations of those who had commercialized the Temple in Jerusalem.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: heavenly army) a large group or throng of angels
senses.comment: There may be distinct objections to speaking of στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as being a ‘heavenly army,’ though undoubtedly in earlier times the thought of angels being God’s military force would have been quite appropriate. Therefore, in place of some expression which may refer to an army or military unit, it may be possible to translate στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as simply ‘many, many angels’ or ‘row after row of angels.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: army of heaven) the stars of heaven as symbols of various supernatural powers
senses.comment: Since ‘the stars of heaven’ serve primarily as symbols of certain heavenly supernatural powers, it may be appropriate in some languages to speak of ‘the spirits of the stars in the sky.’ See also 1.5.

senses.def: to happen, with the implication of occurring in connection with other events
to send someone together with someone else
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult to express in a succinct way the meaning of ‘to send with.’ For example, in 2 Corinthians 8:22 it may be necessary to translate ‘they are going and so we are causing our Christian brother to go with them,’ and in 2 Corinthians 12:18 one may translate ‘I begged Titus to go, and I caused the other Christian brother to go with him.’

senses.def: a city on the east coast of Sicily
an ordered or arranged sequence
a proper and correct order
senses.comment: In Colossians 2:5 τάξις may refer to the orderly manner in which the church at Colossae conducted its affairs or carried on its worship.

senses.def: kind or type of entity, implying a contrast-comparison to other similar entities
senses.comment: It is possible that τάξις in Hebrews 5:6 refers to a kind of priest on the basis of being in a particular grouping or order of priests, but there seems to be no reference to any higher rank or position.

senses.def: to become liquid, either by melting or condensation
third in a series involving either time, space, or set
a third part of an object, series, or mass
senses.comment: In a number of languages a fractional part of something is referred to by means of ordinal numbers. For example, ‘a third of the trees’ would be rendered as ‘every third tree,’ and ‘a third of the earth was consumed by fire’ would be rendered as ‘the third part of the earth was consumed by fire’ or ‘having divided the earth into three parts, one part was destroyed by fire.’

senses.def: pertaining to being legally bound to a man in marriage
capacity to continue to bear up under difficult circumstances
information concerning a person or an event
a payment made by the people of one nation to another, with the implication that this is a symbol of submission and dependence
a location on the surface of the earth
pertaining to being superior for a particular purpose or use
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate Luke 5:39 as ‘the old wine tastes better’ or ‘the old wine is fine to the taste’ or, in an idiomatic expression, ‘the old wine makes the tongue dance.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being useful and benevolent

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of χρηστεύομαι ‘to act kindly,’ 88.67) pertaining to being kind
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘God is kind’ is ‘God is good to’ or ‘God does what is good for.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which is pleasant or easy, with the implication of suitability
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to translate χρηστός by a negativized equivalent, for example, ‘it is not difficult to bear.’

senses.def: any kind of egg, but primarily a chicken egg
senses.comment: In some languages a distinction is made between eggs produced by birds and those produced by such other animals as reptiles and amphibians. In this one NT context the reference is, of course, to the egg of a hen.
